title: Perceptions of health misinformation on social media: patterns and predictors
screen_reason: Secondary analysis of HINTS 7 (2024), a probability address-based survey of US adults; 4,741 of 7,278 respondents had complete data. The outcome item is 'How much of the health information that you see on social media do you think is false or misleading?' with options a lot / some / a little / none, and the paper reports weighted shares: 81.6% a lot or some, 36.4% a lot. This is the instructions' named clause on the perceived amount of misinformation in one's environment, so it licenses RECALL rows (recall_subtype exposure). Both rows are marked borderline: perception of how much of what one sees is false is a judgement about the environment, not a measured or even self-reported encounter with a specific false claim. Everything else in the paper is regression on predictors and is not extracted.

estimates.platform: Social media (unspecified), asked in a national survey
estimates.measure_type: % of US adults who think a lot or some of the health information they see on social media is false or misleading
estimates.value_raw: 3,925 (81.6%) a lot/some vs 816 (18.4%) a little/none, weighted percentages
estimates.denominator: 4,741 HINTS 7 (2024) respondents with complete data on all study variables, out of 7,278 who completed the survey; weighted to US non-institutionalised adults 18+
estimates.definition: Answered 'a lot' or 'some' to 'How much of the health information that you see on social media do you think is false or misleading?' (versus 'a little' or 'none')
estimates.misinfo_def: Health misinformation was described as 'information that is false, inaccurate, or misleading according to the best available evidence at the time'
estimates.source_quote: Exactly 81.6% (weighted percentage) perceived lot/some health misinformation and 18.4% perceived a little/no health misinformation on social media.
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Primary analysis comparing a lot/some vs. a little/none perceived health misinformation'; Tables 1 and 2
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Single self-report item in HINTS 7, administered by the National Cancer Institute; no external verification of what respondents actually saw. Weighted with jackknife replicate weights (R survey/srvyr).
estimates.moderator_quote: Participants were asked, “How much of the health information that you see on social media do you think is false or misleading?” with response options of a lot, some, a little, and none.
estimates.notes: Borderline by construction: this is a perceived share of one's own social media feed, not a report of encountering a specific piece of misinformation, so it belongs in the perceived-environment category the instructions allow rather than with behavioural exposure. Denominator is the complete-case analytic sample (4,741), not the 7,278 who responded, so 35% of respondents are dropped and no non-response adjustment for that loss is described. Platform coded as survey because the item names social media generically with no platform breakdown.

estimates.platform: Social media (unspecified), asked in a national survey
estimates.measure_type: % of US adults who think a lot of the health information they see on social media is false or misleading (stricter threshold)
estimates.value_raw: 1,734 (36.4%) a lot vs 3,007 (63.6%) some/a little/none, weighted percentages
estimates.denominator: 4,741 HINTS 7 (2024) respondents with complete data on all study variables; weighted to US non-institutionalised adults 18+
estimates.definition: Answered 'a lot' (rather than some, a little or none) to 'How much of the health information that you see on social media do you think is false or misleading?'
estimates.misinfo_def: Health misinformation was described as 'information that is false, inaccurate, or misleading according to the best available evidence at the time'
estimates.source_quote: 36.4% (weighted percentage) perceived lot and 63.6% perceived some/a little/no health misinformation on social media.
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Sensitivity analyses comparing "a Lot" to all other categories of perceived health misinformation'; Tables 3 and 4
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same single HINTS 7 self-report item, dichotomised at the stricter threshold for the paper's sensitivity analysis.
estimates.moderator_quote: For the primary analysis, we compared “a lot/some” vs. “a little/none.” As a sensitivity analysis, we further compared “a lot” vs. all other responses (some, a little, and none).
estimates.notes: Stricter cut of the same item as the row above (same country, same platform cell), so definition_variant is true. Same borderline caveat about perception rather than encounter.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (a) every odds ratio in Tables 1-4 (age, education, race/ethnicity, income, trust in the healthcare system, network agreement on health views) - predictors of perception, not prevalence, and the paper is explicit that the analysis is exploratory with backward elimination; (b) the demographic composition of the sample (60% aged 18-49, 51% male, 84% in good or better health) - sample description; (c) the content-analysis percentages quoted in the Introduction from other papers (18% of TikTok pelvic-floor videos containing misinformation, 49% of hypertension YouTube videos misleading, 45% of fertility posts inaccurate, 115/150 (77%) prostate videos biased or poor quality, Pew platform-use figures) - figures cited from elsewhere, excluded by rule. Worth a human's attention: the analytic sample drops 2,537 of 7,278 respondents (35%) for item non-response and the paper does not characterise who was lost, so the weighted 81.6% and 36.4% carry an unquantified complete-case bias; and the outcome is a perception of one's own feed, which the authors themselves treat as a perception rather than an exposure measure ('Perceived health misinformation on social media varies by...').

rob.design: Secondary analysis of HINTS 7, a National Cancer Institute probability survey of non-institutionalised US adults 18+, fielded March-September 2024 by paper and web with a two-stage address-based design (stratified address sample, then one adult per household), a $2 unconditional incentive and a $10 web bonus. 7,278 completed; 4,741 complete cases analysed. Outcome is a single self-report item on how much health information seen on social media is thought to be false or misleading. Weighted percentages with jackknife replicate weights; univariable then multivariable svyglm logistic regression with backward elimination to p < 0.05, candidates screened at p < 0.10. No response rate is reported in the text (it refers readers to the HINTS website), and no ground truth beyond self-report.
